title: Less Red Meat, Lower Impact
body: Eating less red meat is one of the most effective ways to reduce the environmental impact of your diet.

title: Beef and Forests
body: Reducing beef consumption can help lower pressure on forests and natural habitats.

title: Less Meat, Fewer Emissions
body: Diets with less meat generally produce fewer greenhouse gas emissions.

title: More Plants, Less Red Meat
body: Sustainable diets tend to contain more plant foods and less red meat.

title: Beef's Land Footprint
body: Producing beef requires much more land than producing plant proteins such as peas or tofu.

title: Meat and Water Use
body: Eating less meat can reduce water use associated with food production.

title: Meat and Antibiotics
body: Reducing meat consumption may help decrease the need for antibiotics in livestock farming.
source: European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. (n.d)

title: Livestock Land vs. Calories
body: Livestock production uses most agricultural land globally while supplying a much smaller share of calories and protein.

title: Livestock and Biodiversity
body: Lower demand for livestock products can help conserve biodiversity by reducing land conversion.

title: Swap Meat for Legumes
body: Replacing some meat meals with legumes can maintain protein intake while reducing environmental impacts.

title: Legumes Cut Climate Impact
body: Replacing part of your meat intake with legumes can reduce the climate impact of your diet.

title: Pulses: Nutritious and Low-Impact
body: Pulses are rich in protein, fibre, vitamins and minerals while having a low environmental footprint.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2016)

title: Diversify Your Protein
body: Diversifying protein sources helps support both human health and environmental sustainability.

title: Top Sustainable Proteins
body: Beans, lentils, peas and chickpeas are among the most sustainable protein sources available.

title: Pulses Save Water
body: Pulses generally require less water than many animal-based protein sources.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2016)

title: Legumes Plus Cereals
body: Combining legumes with cereals improves the quality of plant protein.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2016)

title: Eggs and Dairy vs. Red Meat
body: Eggs and dairy products can provide protein with a lower environmental impact than red meat.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2016)

title: Pulses Feed the Soil
body: Pulses naturally improve soil fertility by fixing nitrogen from the air, reducing the need for fertilizer.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2016)

title: Insects as Protein
body: Insects are rich in nutrients and may become an important alternative protein source in future food systems.

title: Plant-Based Meat Alternatives
body: Plant-based meat alternatives can help reduce meat consumption, but their nutritional quality varies between products.

title: Quinoa: A Complete Protein
body: Quinoa contains all nine essential amino acids, making it a complete plant protein.

title: Pulses and Chronic Disease
body: Pulses are nutritious staple foods linked to lower risk of chronic diseases.

title: Beyond Wheat, Rice and Maize
body: Alternative crops help reduce dependence on wheat, rice and maize.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2023)

title: Hardy Millets
body: Millets are highly resilient crops that can grow in hot, dry conditions with little water.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2023)

title: Millets in a Changing Climate
body: Millets can continue producing food under climate conditions where other crops may fail.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2023)

title: Diverse Crops, Stronger Food Security
body: Growing more diverse staple crops can strengthen food security and resilience to climate change.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2023)

title: Quinoa Goes Global
body: Quinoa is now cultivated in more than 70 countries, helping diversify global food production.
source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (2023)

title: Buckwheat Benefits
body: Buckwheat is naturally gluten-free and rich in fibre, protein and antioxidants.

title: Amaranth Protein
body: Amaranth contains high-quality protein, including lysine.

title: Antioxidants in Ancient Grains
body: Ancient grains such as millet, quinoa and amaranth contain beneficial antioxidant compounds.

title: Farming Covers Half the Land
body: About half of the world's habitable land is used for agriculture.

title: Plant Protein Saves Land
body: Producing plant proteins generally requires far less land than producing meat.

title: Plant-Based Meals Free Up Land
body: Choosing more plant-based meals can help free land for nature restoration.

title: Less Beef, Less Land
body: Reducing beef consumption is one of the biggest diet changes for lowering land use.

title: Beef Needs the Most Land
body: Beef is one of the most land-intensive foods people consume.

title: Food Waste Wastes Land
body: Reducing food waste could save land larger than some countries.

title: Farming Depends on Nature
body: Agriculture depends on healthy soils, biodiversity and ecosystem services.

title: Land for Livestock and Feed
body: Most agricultural land is used for livestock grazing or growing animal feed.

title: Farmland Expansion and Biodiversity
body: Farmland expansion is a major driver of biodiversity loss.

title: Degraded Farmland
body: Around 52% of agricultural land is moderately or significantly degraded.

title: Agriculture's Water Use
body: Around 70% of global freshwater withdrawals are used for agriculture.

title: Fewer Animal Products, Less Water
body: Diets with fewer animal products often require less water.

title: Sustainable Diets Save Water
body: Sustainable diets can reduce food-related water use by 20–50%.

title: Food Waste Wastes Water
body: Food waste also wastes enormous amounts of water used to grow food.

title: Water Shortages Ahead
body: Water shortages could threaten food production in many regions by 2050.

title: Prevent Waste, Save Water
body: Preventing food waste helps conserve freshwater resources.

title: Your Diet's Water Footprint
body: The water footprint of your diet depends heavily on what you eat.

title: Smarter Water Management
body: Improving water management can reduce the environmental impact of farming.

title: Rising Irrigation
body: Irrigation water use has more than doubled since 1961.

title: Fertilizer and Water Pollution
body: Excess fertilizer use contributes to water pollution and dead zones.

title: Food's Share of Emissions
body: Food systems generate about one-third of global greenhouse gas emissions.

title: Legumes Lower Emissions
body: Replacing some animal protein with legumes can lower dietary emissions.

title: Seasonal Food, Lower Emissions
body: Buying seasonal foods can help reduce food-related emissions.

title: Same Calories, Different Footprints
body: Foods with the same calories can have very different carbon footprints.

title: Beef and Lamb Footprint
body: Meat, especially beef and lamb, has a much higher carbon footprint than most plant foods.

title: Vegetarian Diet Emissions
body: Vegetarian diets can produce substantially fewer emissions than meat-heavy diets.

title: The Flexitarian Effect
body: Flexitarian diets can significantly reduce climate impacts.

title: Emissions from Food Waste
body: Food waste generates billions of tonnes of CO2-equivalent emissions annually.

title: Forests Store Carbon
body: Protecting forests prevents large carbon emissions from land conversion.

title: Legume Crop Rotations
body: Crop rotations with legumes can reduce the carbon footprint of crop production.

title: Emissions from Food Transport
body: Global food transport generates about 3 billion tonnes of CO₂-equivalent emissions each year.

title: Refrigerated Transport
body: Long-distance transport often requires refrigeration, which increases the energy use and carbon footprint of food.

title: Seasonal Choices, Less Transport
body: Choosing seasonal foods and reducing unnecessary transport can help lower the climate impact of the food system.

title: Transport's Share of Food Emissions
body: Nearly one-fifth of the greenhouse gas emissions from the global food system come from transporting food.

title: Food Miles of Fruit and Veg
body: Fruit and vegetables account for around 36% of food-mile emissions worldwide.

title: The Cold Chain
body: Maintaining an unbroken cold chain is essential for preserving food quality and reducing spoilage during transport.

title: Transport vs. Growing Emissions
body: Transporting fruit and vegetables can generate roughly twice the greenhouse gas emissions produced during their cultivation.

title: Food Freight Emissions
body: Although food accounts for only about 18% of global freight transport distances, it produces around 27% of freight-related emissions.

title: Food Lost Without Cooling
body: Around 526 million tonnes of food are lost or wasted each year because of inadequate refrigeration and cooling systems.

title: Better Cold Chains
body: Improving cold-chain infrastructure can reduce food losses, improve food security, and reduce environmental impacts.

title: Processing for Safety
body: Food processing can improve food safety and extend shelf life.

title: Processing Prevents Waste
body: Processing can help reduce food waste by preserving food for longer.

title: Ultra-Processed Foods
body: Ultra-processed foods are often higher in sugar, salt and saturated fat.

title: Processing Energy Use
body: Different processing methods use very different amounts of energy.

title: Frozen Food Energy
body: Frozen foods can require substantial energy for storage.

title: Beyond the Farm Gate
body: Processing, packaging and transport all contribute to food-system impacts.

title: Not All Processing Is Harmful
body: Not all processed foods have high environmental impacts.

title: Efficient Storage and Transport
body: Food processing can improve storage and transport efficiency.

title: Technology Matters
body: The sustainability of processed foods depends on production technology.

title: The Full Life Cycle
body: Looking at the full food life cycle gives a better sustainability picture than focusing only on processing.

title: Short Supply Chains
body: Short supply chains can support local economies and resilience.

title: Seasonal and Local
body: Seasonal local food may reduce storage and transport requirements.

title: Origin Isn't Everything
body: Country of origin alone cannot determine whether a food is sustainable.

title: Origin and Traceability
body: Food origin can provide useful information about traceability and sustainability.

title: Booming Food Trade
body: Global food trade has increased dramatically over recent decades.

title: Europe's Imported Feed
body: Many European food systems depend on imported feed and commodities.

title: Trust in Origin Labels
body: Consumers often associate origin labels with quality and safety.

title: Local Isn't Always Greener
body: Local food is not always the most sustainable option.

title: How Beats How Far
body: How food is produced often matters more than the distance it travels.

title: Air vs. Sea Freight
body: Air-freighted food can have a much larger carbon footprint than sea-freighted food.

title: Organic Farms and Biodiversity
body: Organic farms support higher biodiversity than conventional farms.

title: Climate-Smart Agriculture
body: Climate-smart agriculture aims to improve resilience while reducing emissions.

title: Balanced Farming
body: Sustainable farming balances productivity with environmental protection.

title: Flower Strips for Pollinators
body: Flower strips and pollinator habitats can support biodiversity on farms.

title: Organic Without Synthetics
body: Organic farming avoids synthetic fertilizers and pesticides.

title: Crop Diversification
body: Crop diversification helps farms resist pests and diseases.

title: Agroforestry
body: Agroforestry combines trees with crops or livestock on the same land.

title: Integrated Pest Management
body: Integrated Pest Management reduces reliance on chemical pesticides.

title: Precision Agriculture
body: Precision agriculture can reduce fertilizer use and emissions.

title: Conservation Agriculture
body: Conservation agriculture reduces soil disturbance and protects soil health.

title: Diverse Crops and Breeds
body: Diversifying crops and breeds can increase food-system resilience.

title: Alternative Proteins
body: Alternative proteins may reduce reliance on conventional livestock production.

title: Breeding in Context
body: Sustainable breeding should be combined with broader food-system improvements.

title: Low-Methane Breeding
body: Breeding animals for lower methane emissions can reduce livestock impacts.

title: Alternative Fish Feeds
body: Alternative aquaculture feeds can reduce pressure on wild fish stocks.

title: Climate-Ready Crops
body: Genetic improvement can help crops cope with new environmental challenges.

title: Productive Livestock
body: Improving animal productivity can reduce resource use per kilogram of meat.

title: Genome Editing
body: Genome editing may help develop crops that are more resilient to climate stress.

title: Feed-Efficient Livestock
body: Selective breeding can improve feed efficiency in livestock.

title: Hydroponics and Aquaponics
body: Hydroponic and aquaponic systems can use far less water than conventional farming.

title: Child Labour in Agriculture
body: Agriculture accounts for most child labour cases worldwide.

title: Fairtrade for Farmers
body: Fairtrade aims to improve incomes and working conditions for farmers.

title: Fair Pricing
body: Fair trade promotes transparency and fair pricing across supply chains.

title: Decent Working Conditions
body: Safe and decent working conditions are a key part of sustainable food systems.

title: Social Sustainability
body: Food-system sustainability includes social and labour conditions.

title: Vulnerable Food Workers
body: Many food-system workers remain vulnerable to exploitation.

title: Ethical Food Choices
body: Consumers increasingly value ethical and fair food production.

title: Women in Food Production
body: Women play a critical role in food production but often have less access to resources.

title: Smallholder Farmers
body: Smallholder farmers produce a large share of the world's food.

title: Sound and Just Food Systems
body: Sustainable food systems should be environmentally sound and socially just.

title: Why Packaging Matters
body: Food packaging protects products from contamination, moisture, oxygen and physical damage, helping maintain food safety and quality.

title: Plastic Prevents Spoilage
body: Plastic packaging can reduce food spoilage because it is lightweight, durable and effective at protecting perishable foods.

title: Balanced Packaging
body: The most sustainable packaging balances material efficiency, recyclability, product protection and food-waste prevention.

title: Food vs. Packaging Impact
body: The environmental impact of producing food is often much greater than the impact of the packaging used to protect it.

title: Packaging Against Waste
body: Well-designed packaging can reduce food waste by extending shelf life and preventing spoilage during transport, storage and home use.

title: No Perfect Packaging
body: There is no single “most sustainable” packaging material; environmental performance depends on the entire product life cycle.

title: Edible Packaging
body: Edible packaging can help reduce reliance on fossil-based plastics by replacing conventional packaging materials with biodegradable alternatives.

title: Edible Coatings
body: Edible coatings can extend the shelf life of fruits and vegetables by reducing moisture loss and slowing respiration.

title: Smart Packaging
body: Smart packaging can monitor temperature, freshness and product condition, helping reduce food losses across the supply chain.

title: Active Packaging
body: Active packaging can interact with food by absorbing oxygen or moisture, helping products stay fresh for longer.

title: Reuse Pays Off Over Time
body: Reusable packaging only becomes environmentally beneficial after it has been reused enough times.

title: Europe's Packaging Waste
body: Europe generates about 1.5 tonnes of single-use packaging waste every second.

title: Packaging Recycling Rates
body: Only around 40% of packaging waste in Europe is recycled.

title: Reuse Saves Raw Materials
body: Reusable packaging can reduce demand for virgin raw materials.

title: Reuse Frequency Matters
body: The environmental benefits of reusable packaging depend on how often it is reused.

title: Transport and Cleaning
body: Transport distances and cleaning processes influence the environmental impact of reusable packaging systems.

title: The Break-Even Point
body: Every reusable package has a break-even point where it becomes better than single-use alternatives.

title: High Return Rates
body: Many reuse systems in Europe already achieve return rates of 75% or higher.

title: Packaging Extends Shelf Life
body: Improved packaging systems can help reduce food waste by extending shelf life.

title: Long-Lasting Transport Packaging
body: Reusable transport packaging is often designed to remain in circulation for many years.

title: Households Waste the Most
body: Households generate more food waste than any other sector in the European Union.

title: One-Fifth Wasted
body: Around one fifth of food available to consumers is wasted globally.

title: Lists and Meal Plans
body: Shopping lists and meal planning can help reduce food waste at home.

title: Smaller Portions, Less Waste
body: Offering smaller portion sizes can reduce plate waste in canteens and restaurants.

title: Standard Portions, More Leftovers
body: Standard portion sizes often lead to unnecessary leftovers.

title: Buffet Overload
body: Many people take more food than they can eat in buffet-style dining environments.

title: Waste and Climate
body: Food waste is responsible for a significant share of food-system greenhouse gas emissions.

title: Wasted Meat
body: Wasted meat contributes disproportionately to the climate impact of food waste.

title: If Food Waste Were a Country
body: If food waste were a country, it would be one of the world’s largest greenhouse gas emitters.

title: Wasted Nutrients
body: Wasted food also means wasted nutrients such as protein and fibre.

title: Waste Starts at Home
body: Households account for more than half of food waste generated in the EU.

title: Store Food Properly
body: Proper storage helps reduce waste and keeps food safe to eat.

title: The Two-Hour Rule
body: Perishable foods should generally not be left at room temperature for more than two hours.

title: Plan and Reuse Leftovers
body: Better planning and reuse of leftovers can save money and reduce environmental impacts.

title: Best Before vs. Use By
body: Best-before dates refer to quality, while use-by dates refer to food safety.

title: Most Wasted Foods
body: Fruits and vegetables are the most wasted foods in Europe.

title: Cool Leftovers Quickly
body: Cooling leftovers quickly helps prevent bacterial growth.

title: Wasted Meat and Dairy
body: Meat and dairy may be wasted less often but have a larger environmental footprint when wasted.

title: Divide to Cool
body: Large portions of food cool faster when divided into smaller containers.

title: Airtight Containers
body: Airtight containers help keep leftovers fresh for longer.

title: Households Lead Food Waste
body: More than half of all food waste in Europe is generated by households.

title: Overbuying
body: Buying more food than needed is one of the main causes of avoidable food waste at home.

title: Check Before You Shop
body: Planning meals and checking cupboards before shopping can help reduce overbuying and food waste.

title: Freeze Surplus Food
body: Freezing surplus food before it spoils can extend its shelf life and reduce waste.

title: 69 Million Tonnes
body: Household food waste in Europe is estimated at around 69 million tonnes per year.

title: Date Label Confusion
body: Confusion about “best before” and “use by” labels contributes significantly to unnecessary food waste.

title: Safe After Best Before
body: Many foods remain safe to eat after their “best before” date if they have been stored correctly.

title: Multi-Buy Traps
body: Multi-buy offers and bulk discounts can encourage consumers to purchase more food than they can use.

title: Commonly Overbought Foods
body: Fresh fruit, vegetables, dairy products and bakery items are among the foods most commonly wasted because of over-purchasing.

title: Track Your Waste
body: Keeping track of the food you throw away can help identify habits that lead to overconsumption and waste.

title: Growing Portions
body: Portion sizes in many countries have increased substantially over recent decades.

title: Bigger Portions, Not Fuller
body: Larger portion sizes often lead people to eat more without feeling proportionally fuller.

title: Healthy for You and the Planet
body: Reducing excessive food intake can benefit both personal health and environmental sustainability.

title: How Much You Eat Matters
body: The environmental impact of a diet depends not only on what people eat but also on how much they eat.

title: Excess Calories, More Emissions
body: Consuming excess calories contributes to higher food-system greenhouse gas emissions because more food must be produced.

title: High-Impact Foods in Excess
body: Foods with high environmental footprints have an even greater impact when consumed in excess.

title: Right-Sized Portions
body: Choosing appropriate portion sizes can help reduce both calorie overconsumption and resource use.

title: Overeating Uses Resources
body: Eating more food than the body needs increases demand for agricultural resources such as land, water and energy.

title: Overconsumption's Ripple Effect
body: Overconsumption contributes to unnecessary demand for food production, transport, storage and packaging.

title: Enough, Not Excess
body: Sustainable diets encourage eating enough to meet nutritional needs while avoiding excessive consumption.

title: What Protein Does
body: Protein helps build and repair muscles, tissues, enzymes and hormones.

title: Plant and Animal Protein
body: Both plant and animal foods can provide protein.

title: Legumes for Health and Planet
body: Replacing some red meat with legumes benefits health and sustainability.

title: How Much Protein You Need
body: Most adults need about 0.83 g of protein per kilogram of body weight each day.

title: Plant Protein Sources
body: Lentils, beans, peas, nuts and seeds are excellent plant protein sources.

title: The Whole Nutritional Package
body: The overall nutritional package of a protein source matters, not just its protein content.

title: Mix Your Plant Proteins
body: Eating a variety of plant proteins can provide all essential amino acids.

title: Quinoa's Amino Acids
body: Quinoa is a complete plant protein containing all essential amino acids.

title: Protein Quality
body: Protein quality depends on digestibility and amino acid composition.

title: Too Much Protein
body: Many high-income countries consume more protein than recommended.

title: Unsaturated vs. Saturated Fats
body: Unsaturated fats are generally healthier than saturated fats.

title: Limit Saturated Fat
body: WHO recommends limiting saturated fat to less than 10% of daily energy intake.

title: Healthy Fat Sources
body: Nuts, seeds, fish and olive oil are good sources of healthy fats.

title: Fat Type Matters
body: The type of fat you eat matters as much as the amount.

title: Avoid Trans Fats
body: Trans fats increase the risk of heart disease and have no known health benefits.

title: Swap Fats for Heart Health
body: Replacing saturated fat with unsaturated fat can improve heart health.

title: How Much Fat
body: Fat should contribute no more than about 30% of total daily energy intake.

title: Low-Fat, High-Sugar
body: Low-fat processed foods may still contain high levels of sugar.

title: Removing Trans Fats
body: Industrially produced trans fats can be removed without affecting food availability.

title: Fat and Vitamins
body: Fat helps the body absorb vitamins A, D, E and K.

title: Sugary Drinks
body: Sugary drinks are a major source of added sugar in many diets.

title: Sugar and Teeth
body: High sugar intake contributes to tooth decay.

title: Sugar and Weight
body: Excess sugar intake is linked to weight gain and obesity.

title: Limit Free Sugars
body: WHO recommends limiting free sugars to less than 10% of daily energy intake.

title: Sugar in Fruit
body: Fruit contains natural sugars together with fibre and vitamins.

title: Cut Sugary Drinks
body: Reducing sugary drink consumption is an effective way to lower sugar intake.

title: Cook to Control Sugar
body: Cooking at home makes it easier to control added sugar.

title: Empty Calories
body: Sugar provides energy but few essential nutrients.

title: Below 5% Sugar
body: Reducing free sugars to below 5% may provide additional health benefits.

title: Spot Added Sugar
body: Reading labels can help identify foods high in added sugar.

title: Too Much Salt
body: Most people consume more than twice the recommended salt intake.

title: Salt and Heart Health
body: Reducing salt intake lowers the risk of heart disease and stroke.

title: Sodium's Global Toll
body: Excess sodium intake contributes to millions of deaths worldwide.

title: Under 5 Grams of Salt
body: WHO recommends consuming less than 5 grams of salt per day.

title: Hidden Salt
body: Most dietary salt comes from processed and restaurant foods.

title: Sodium and Blood Pressure
body: High sodium intake increases blood pressure.

title: Herbs Instead of Salt
body: Herbs and spices can help replace salt in cooking.

title: Europe's Sodium Sources
body: Bread, processed meat and cheese are major sodium sources in Europe.

title: Salt Substitutes
body: Low-sodium salt substitutes may help suitable adults reduce sodium intake.

title: All Salt Is Sodium
body: Sea salt, Himalayan salt and table salt all contain significant sodium.

title: The Fibre Gap
body: Most Europeans consume less fibre than recommended.

title: Fibre Sources
body: Whole grains, fruits, vegetables and pulses are excellent fibre sources.

title: Water and Fibre
body: Drinking enough water helps fibre work effectively.

title: 25 Grams a Day
body: Adults should aim for at least 25 grams of fibre per day.

title: Increase Fibre Gradually
body: Increasing fibre gradually can reduce digestive discomfort.

title: Whole Grain Goodness
body: Whole grains provide fibre as well as important nutrients.

title: Fibre for Digestion
body: Fibre supports healthy digestion and bowel function.

title: Fibre and Disease Risk
body: Higher fibre intake is linked to lower risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes.

title: Soluble and Insoluble Fibre
body: Both soluble and insoluble fibre contribute to health.

title: Fibre Keeps You Full
body: Fibre-rich foods can help people feel full for longer.

title: Vitamin D Deficiency
body: Vitamin D deficiency is common across Europe.

title: Vitamin C
body: Vitamin C supports immunity and wound healing.

title: Vitamins from Produce
body: Fruits and vegetables provide important vitamins and antioxidants.

title: Diversity Prevents Deficiency
body: Eating a diverse diet helps reduce the risk of vitamin deficiencies.

title: Vitamin A Sources
body: Orange and dark-green vegetables are good sources of vitamin A precursors.

title: Vitamin E Sources
body: Nuts, seeds and vegetable oils are good sources of vitamin E.

title: Sunlight and Vitamin D
body: Sunlight is the body’s primary source of vitamin D.

title: Vitamin B12 Sources
body: Vitamin B12 is found mainly in animal-based foods.

title: B12 for Vegans
body: Vegans may need fortified foods or supplements to obtain enough B12.

title: Hidden Hunger
body: Vitamin deficiencies can occur even when food is abundant.

title: Enough Calories for All
body: The world already produces enough calories to feed everyone.

title: Nutrients vs. Calories
body: Nutrient-rich foods are not always the same as calorie-rich foods.

title: Ultra-Processed and Overeating
body: Ultra-processed foods may encourage people to consume more calories.

title: Equal Calories, Unequal Impact
body: Foods providing the same number of calories can have very different environmental impacts.

title: Beyond Counting Calories
body: Sustainable diets focus on food choices, not only calorie reduction.

title: Calories Lost Farm to Plate
body: More than half of food calories are lost between farm and plate.

title: The Big Three Staples
body: Rice, wheat and maize provide nearly half of global calories.

title: Feed Crop Losses
body: Feeding crops to livestock results in major calorie losses.

title: Beef Emissions per Calorie
body: Beef generates far more emissions per calorie than most plant foods.

title: Efficient Food Systems
body: Improving food-system efficiency can increase available nutrition without producing more food.
